messages.author: 6b41239f795f4a4c
messages.subject: Stan with large data
parts:
Hi,
Is there any experiences using Stan on a regression model with 10^3 outcomes and 10^4 or 10^5 predictors? I am interested to know if you think it will be able to handle that many parameters and how much memory and time would take to process a model of that size.

BW,
Inti

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan with large data
parts:
10^3 categorical outcomes is going to be a problem with
a lot of predictors if the predictors are sparse.

Stan scales with the number of subexpressions in the
evaluation of the log probability, so if the predictors
are dense and you have to evaluate (10^5 * 10^3) = 10^8
multiplications per data point, it's going to be very very slow
pretty much no matter what you do. And Stan will blow out
memory if you try to do that, because we require on the order
of 24 bytes per subexpression storage.

You might want to try something like Vowpal Wabbit, which
can stream the data. It can also help if the data's sparse
among a large potential set of predictors (things
like all 5-character sequences in Unicode) because it allows
a lower-dimensional representation.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan with large data
parts:
I'm assuming the poster meant a 10^3 = 1000-dimensional multi-logit.
Then if there are 10^5 predictors and they're dense, you're
looking at 10^8 multiplications per data point!

10^3 outcomes show up all the time if you're trying to do something
like predict which tag a user will attach to a post. You get 10^5 or
so if you're trying to attach ICD-10 codes to a patient's medical
record. And lots of predictors from the natural language plus
database content.

Yes, we've fit models with 10^6 predictors and with 10^6 data
points, but IRT is very sparse. Binary outputs with three parameters
per data point (discriminativeness of item, difficulty of item,
ability of student, with outcome being correctness of answer).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan with large data
parts:
Hi,
Sorry for the ambiguity. I am interested on a LASSO-type variable selection model. I am actually interested on a model:

Y = b_0 + GBX + Zu + e

with Y and nx1 matrix, X and nxk predictor's matrix, B a vector of coefficients and G a vector indicator variables which formally are the probability of the predictor to be associated with the outcome. The indicator variables generates the simplest form of the peak and slab prior.
The model was presented on Hanni P. Kärkkäinen and Mikko J. Sillanpää "Back to Basics for Bayesian Model Building in Genomic Selection" (http://www.genetics.org/content/191/3/969.abstract). Z diagonal matrix (when the Y observations are iid) and u ~ N(0,A*sigma_u) with A a symmetric dense matrix with A_{ij} being a distance measure between the y_{i} and y_{j} observation. In my application Y are observations for individuals and the matrix A measures the relatedness between individuals (e.g., 0.5 between siblings or 0.125 between cousins) and it is important on this models.

The authors presented a Generalised Expextation Maximisation algorithm to fit the model and obtain MAP estimates making use of conjugate priors through  but the MAP estimates underestimate the uncertainty of the B and G parameters and leads to overoptimistic results, i.e., too many false positives. I know the same model using MCMC leads to appropriate estimates.

In particular I am interested on extending the above model with a second level regression on the indicator variables, like
G ~ t_0 + TH (this would in practice be a probit or logistic model to link this linear predictor to a 0 to 1 variable)
with H a kxp matrix of predictor covariates and T the corresponding coefficients linking the predictor's covariates to the predictor's indicator variables. The idea is to allow the G indicator variables to borrow information from other predictors with similar covariates.

On a real data the dimensions would be:
n = 10^3 - 10^4
k = 10^4 - 10^6
p = 10^2


The X matrix would have predictors with values between 0 and 2 that are normalized to have mean = 0 and variance = 1.

So, more detailed questions:
1- Do you think STAN will be able to work on this model? Do you have any examples of code for this?
2- If the answer to 1 is yes, Any suggestions on what to do or not to do to implement this model?
3- On the extended model I am interested on I think I should be able to sample the T coefficients and the predictor variables G would become determined, so that could reduce the number of parameters. Is that thinking right ?


Thanks a lot in advance for your help,

PS: A similar model to Y = b_0 + GBX + Zu + e was presented by Xiang Zhou et al (http://www.plosgenetics.org/article/info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pgen.1003264).

Yes, we've fit models with 10^6 predictors and with 10^6 data

Andrew's got issues with these priors:

http://andrewgelman.com/2012/09/07/prior-distributions-for-regression-coefficients/

If the spike really is a delta function, Stan has problems
because it intrinsically involves sampling from a discrete
distribution, which Stan doesn't do. So you can't explicitly
model a discrete unknown indicator in Stan.

Without a true delta-function spike, there will be zero
probability mass associated with coeff=0. Is that OK?

> The model was presented on Hanni P. K�rkk�inen and Mikko J. Sillanp�� "Back to Basics for Bayesian Model Building in

> Genomic Selection" (http://www.genetics.org/content/191/3/969.abstract). Z diagonal matrix (when the Y observations are
> iid) and u ~ N(0,A*sigma_u) with A a symmetric dense matrix with A_{ij} being a distance measure between the y_{i} and
> y_{j} observation. In my application Y are observations for individuals and the matrix A measures the relatedness
> between individuals (e.g., 0.5 between siblings or 0.125 between cousins) and it is important on this models.

Right --- that's typical of linkage analyses and shouldn't itself
be an issue.

> The authors presented a Generalised Expextation Maximisation algorithm to fit the model and obtain MAP estimates making
> use of conjugate priors through but the MAP estimates underestimate the uncertainty of the B and G parameters and leads
> to overoptimistic results, i.e., too many false positives. I know the same model using MCMC leads to appropriate estimates.
>
> In particular I am interested on extending the above model with a second level regression on the indicator variables, like
> G ~ t_0 + TH (this would in practice be a probit or logistic model to link this linear predictor to a 0 to 1 variable)
I'd stick to logistic for efficiency.

> with H a kxp matrix of predictor covariates and T the corresponding coefficients linking the predictor's covariates to
> the predictor's indicator variables. The idea is to allow the G indicator variables to borrow information from other
> predictors with similar covariates.
>

> n = 10^3 - 10^4

I think it's going to be close with 10^4 to 10^6 predictors.
That's k * n multiply-adds required for the basic regression for
each log prob evaluation --- at the low end, that's 10M and
at the high end of your ranges, it's 10G. Assuming you pack
this into matrix multiplies, the lower end will fit in memory,
but the higher end almost certainly not.

What's p? Is that the dimensionalty of the second level regression?

> The X matrix would have predictors with values between 0 and 2 that are normalized to have mean = 0 and variance = 1.
>
> So, more detailed questions:
> 1- Do you think STAN will be able to work on this model? Do you have any examples of code for this?

We have lots of hierarchical regression models, but not this specific one.
There are all the ARM models from Jennifer and Andrew's book. There
are simpler ones in the manual, and some that are in between in the BUGS
examples.
> 2- If the answer to 1 is yes, Any suggestions on what to do or not to do to implement this model?

See above.

Also, you're going to want to use the Matt trick (see the
reparameterization/transforms chapter of the manual).

> 3- On the extended model I am interested on I think I should be able to sample the T coefficients and the predictor
> variables G would become determined, so that could reduce the number of parameters. Is that thinking right ?
They all get done at once in Stan.

> Thanks a lot in advance for your help,
>
> PS: A similar model to Y = b_0 + GBX + Zu + e was presented by Xiang Zhou et al
> (http://www.plosgenetics.org/article/info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pgen.1003264).

Thanks for the papers. I should look some of these up
to produce more regression examples (though with less
data).

Also, you can fit posterior mode estimates using Stan's optimizers.
Very tricky with hierarchical models, though --- you really want
to integrate out the variances that would otherwise go to 0 in
the posterior modes.

- Bob

messages.author: 146bc26797d1c5e2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan with large data
parts:
The spike in the original spike and slab is not a true delta function, although its role is certainly that of a delta, that is, to represent coefficients that are practically zero. 

Spike and slab could well be a realistic prior in some applications. Genetics ((maybe too) broadly speaking) is an obvious example. Even if it is not realistic, it may be practical, if models with such a prior can be estimated. Results from models with a huge number of potential predictors are kind of work hypotheses anyway. They point to possible effects that should be further tested and quantified. 

(I have played with doubly hierarchical Cauchy priors in Stan months ago, and was surprised of their power to choose variables form simulated data with a large number of predictors, around 1–10x number of samples. None of the priors was probably not the true spike and slab, though. The Cauchy geometry is hard for Stan, or HMC or almost any sampler, so these might be difficult to get scaled to large data. messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: [stan-users] I hate the slab
parts:
This is getting off-topic, but . . . let me say that the "spike" may be reasonable in various settings where there are many small effects that are indistinguishable from 0. My problem is more with the "slab." Real, nonzero effects still tend to be concentrated not toooo far from 0. I like lasso because it does some partial pooling. The slab doesn't do any pooling at all.
A

P.S. If you really want to work with Cauchy models in Stan, perhaps it would make sense to hard-code a reparameterization so that the distribution has a more reasonable tails in the transformed space.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan with large data
parts:
Unfortunately I don't remember details related to the speed of spikeSlabGAM. I had 8000 samples and the number of predictors varied in hundreds, and it was not inconveniently slow, at most tens of minutes (or a couple of hours?) per run. 

spikeSlabGAM has a hierarchy that pools related parameters, i.e., those that are of a particular spline, variable, interaction or random effect. So the prior is somewhat modified from the original spike and slab, but probably not the way Andrew suggests. 

I have no affiliation with either the spike or the slab… but an ultra-concave prior does seem useful sometimes.

There is also a machine learning paper in which a sampler with spike-and-slab priors outperformed L1 with CV, under a fixed CPU budget: http://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.1157.pdf
